In mathematics, the '''trace field''' of a [[linear group]] is the field generated by the [[Trace (linear algebra)|traces]] of its elements. It is mostly studied for [[Kleinian group|Kleinian]] and [[Fuchsian group]]s, though related objects are used in the theory of [[Lattice (discrete subgroup)|lattices]] in Lie groups, often under the name ''field of definition''.

== Fuchsian and Kleinian groups ==

=== Trace field and invariant trace fields for Fuchsian groups ===

Fuchsian groups are discrete subgroups of <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)</math>. The trace of an element in <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)</math> is well-defined up to sign (by taking the trace of an arbitrary preimage in <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)</math>) and the ''trace field'' of <math>\Gamma</math> is the field generated over <math>\mathbb Q</math> by the traces of all elements of <math>\Gamma</math> (see for example in {{harvtxt|Maclachlan|Reid|2003}}).

The ''invariant trace field'' is equal to the trace field of the subgroup <math>\Gamma^{(2)}</math> generated by all squares of elements of <math>\Gamma</math> (a finite-index subgroup of <math>\Gamma</math>).{{sfn|Maclachlan|Reid|2003|loc=Chapter 3.3}}

The invariant trace field of Fuchsian groups is stable under taking [[Commensurability (group theory)|commensurable]] groups. This is not the case for the trace field;{{sfn|Maclachlan|Reid|2003|loc=Example 3.3.1}} in particular the trace field is in general different from the invariant trace field.

=== Quaternion algebras for Fuchsian groups ===

Let <math>\Gamma</math> be a Fuchsian group and <math>k</math> its trace field. Let <math>A</math> be the <math>k</math>-subalgebra of the matrix algebra <math>M_2(\mathbb R)</math> generated by the preimages of elements of <math>\Gamma</math>. The algebra <math>A</math> is then as simple as possible, more precisely:{{sfn|Maclachlan|Reid|2003|loc=Theorem 3.2.1}}

:''If <math>\Gamma</math> is of the [[Fuchsian group#Limit set|first or second type]] then <math>A</math> is a [[quaternion algebra]] over <math>k</math>. ''

The algebra <math>A</math> is called the quaternion algebra of <math>\Gamma</math>. The quaternion algebra of <math>\Gamma^{(2)}</math> is called the ''invariant quaternion algebra'' of <math>\Gamma</math>, denoted by <math>A\Gamma</math>. As for trace fields, the former is not the same for all groups in the same commensurability class but the latter is.

If <math>\Gamma</math> is an [[arithmetic Fuchsian group]] then <math>k\Gamma</math> and <math>A\Gamma</math> together are a number field and quaternion algebra from which a group commensurable to <math>\Gamma</math> may be derived.{{sfn|Maclachlan|Reid|2003|loc=Chapter 8.4}}

=== Kleinian groups ===

The theory for [[Kleinian group]]s (discrete subgroups of <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)</math>) is mostly similar as that for Fuchsian groups.{{sfn|Maclachlan|Reid|2003|loc=Chapter 3}} One big difference is that the trace field of a group of finite covolume is always a number field.{{sfn|Maclachlan|Reid|2003|loc=Theorem 3.1.2}}

== Trace fields and fields of definition for subgroups of Lie groups ==

=== Definition ===

When considering subgroups of general [[Lie group]]s (which are not necessarily defined as a [[matrix group]]s) one has to use a linear representation of the group to take traces of elements. The most natural one is the [[adjoint representation]]. It turns out that for applications it is better, even for groups which have a natural lower-dimensional linear representation (such as the [[special linear group]]s <math>\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb R)</math>), to always define the trace field using the adjoint representation. Thus we have the following definition, originally due to [[Ernest Vinberg]],{{sfn|Vinberg|1971}} who used the terminology "field of definition".{{sfn|Margulis|1991|loc=Chapter VIII}}

:''Let <math>G</math> be a Lie group and <math>\Gamma \subset G</math> a subgroup. Let <math>\rho</math> be the adjoint representation of <math>G</math>. The trace field of <math>\Gamma</math> is the field:''
::<math> k\Gamma = \mathbb Q(\{ \operatorname{trace}(\rho(\gamma)) : \gamma \in \Gamma \}). </math>

If two [[Zariski topology|Zariski-dense]] subgroups of <math>G</math> are commensurable then they have the same trace field in this sense.

=== The trace field for lattices ===

Let <math>G</math> be a [[semisimple Lie group]] and <math>\Gamma \subset G</math> a [[Lattice (discrete subgroup)|lattice]]. Suppose further that either <math>\Gamma</math> is irreducible and <math>G</math> is not locally isomorphic to <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)</math>, or that <math>\Gamma</math> has no factor [[Lie group#The Lie algebra associated with a Lie group|locally isomorphic]] to <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)</math>. Then [[local rigidity]] implies the following result.

:''The field <math>k\Gamma</math> is a [[number field]]. ''

Furthermore, there exists an [[algebraic group]] <math>\mathbf G</math> over <math>k\Gamma</math> such that the group of [[Rational point#Rational points of schemes|real points]] <math>\mathbf G(\mathbb R)</math> is isomorphic to <math>\rho(G)</math> and <math>\rho(\Gamma)</math> is contained in a conjugate of <math>\mathbf G(k\Gamma)</math>.{{sfn|Vinberg|1971}}{{sfn|Margulis|1991|loc=Chapter VIII, proposition 3.22}} Thus <math>k\Gamma</math> is a "field of definition" for <math>\Gamma</math> in the sense that it is a [[field of definition]] of its [[Zariski topology|Zariski closure]] in the adjoint representation.

In the case where <math>\Gamma</math> is [[Arithmetic group|arithmetic]] then it is commensurable to the arithmetic group defined by <math>\mathbf G</math>.

For Fuchsian groups the field <matH>k\Gamma</math> defined above is equal to its invariant trace field. For Kleinian groups they are the same if we use the adjoint representation over the complex numbers.{{sfn|Maclachlan|Reid|2003|p=321}}
